problem: Zero-shot VLN-CE methods either depend on pre-trained waypoint predictors (12-view RGB-D, poor generalization) or query large models several times per step (STRIDER 3 calls, LaViRA 2), causing high latency. MLLMs also lack metric spatial ability for picking waypoints in graph-free continuous space.
motivation: Real-robot deployment needs low per-step latency and compute. A single-call design is efficient but risks prompt overload and weak spatial grounding, so the waypoint interface must give the MLLM concrete spatial and memory cues.
key_idea: Sample sparse waypoints along the topological skeleton of a global traversability map, project them (color-coded visited vs. unvisited, with IDs) onto four-view RGB images, and let one MLLM call per step choose a waypoint ID or a fallback bounding box, executed by an FMM planner.
insight: The gains come mainly from the waypoint interface rather than the backbone. Under an identical GPT-4o pipeline, the O2C generator beats SmartWay and STRIDER (SR 45.0 vs 35.3 and 26.7). Ablations show that distinguishing visited waypoints and a moderate d_sample=0.5 matter, and that the bbox fallback adds +5 SR. Failure analysis shows 36 of 54 failures are waypoint-selection errors, so the bottleneck is MLLM reasoning rather than candidate coverage.
method: Single-MLLM navigator: one call per step takes instruction, sliding-window history (w=5, with loop warning via a visit counter), four visualized views and a Grounding DINO object list, and outputs an action in {front,left,right,back,stop} plus a waypoint ID or bounding box.

Mapping and navigable region: back-project depth with intrinsics and pose into a 2D semantic top-down grid map, extract a walkable mask, and merge reached positions into visited waypoints if closer than δ.

Topological skeletonization: morphological closing then medial-axis thinning (Zhang-Suen style) gives a 1-pixel skeleton; endpoints (deg=1) and junctions (deg>2) are kept and NMS sampling at d_sample=0.5 m enforces sparsity, followed by erosion for a 0.10 m safety margin.
Abstract waypoint representation: project candidate (cyan) and visited (red) waypoints onto the 4 RGB views with numeric IDs, giving explicit spatial and historical cues.
Bounding-box fallback: if no candidate exists in the chosen direction, the MLLM outputs a bbox whose bottom-center is used as the target.
Low-level control: back-project the target pixel to world coordinates, then an FMM planner on the traversability cost map produces a collision-free path decomposed into discrete actions.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o / Gemini-2.5-Pro / Qwen3-VL-235B / GPT-5.1 / Qwen3-VL-32B (frozen MLLM) + Grounding DINO + FMM planner
setting.action_space: waypoint/bbox target converted by FMM into discrete low-level motor actions
setting.simulator: Habitat (Matterport3D scenes, VLN-CE); real world with Unitree Go2

results: On a 100-episode R2R-CE subset, O2C-Nav with Gemini-2.5-Pro reaches SR 49.3 and OSR 65.0, versus STRIDER (3 calls) SR 35 and LaViRA 38.3. It uses one call per step and achieves the best SPL (31.2 with GPT-4o). On RxR-CE it gets SR 28.4 and SPL 18.7, beating LaViRA (21.3 / 13.3). End-to-end latency on Jetson is 19.58 s versus 24.82 s (SmartWay) and 37.72 s (STRIDER); real-world success is 5/10 on both VLN and ObjectNav.
limitations: Four-view observations lose perspective information and can omit candidate waypoints, yielding low NDTW (about 42 vs 57.7 for Three-Step-Nav).
MLLM hallucination and waypoint-selection errors dominate failures (36/54), and stairs are poorly covered.
Evaluation uses small random subsets (100 R2R-CE episodes), real-world trials are few (10 per task), and per-step latency stays high (19.6 s).
